item.title: Indefinite causal order with definite Bohmian trajectories for the quantum switch
item.description: arXiv:2611.17906v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We analyze the notion of indefinite causal order (ICO) from the standpoint of the deterministic de Broglie--Bohm theory, based on the notion of trajectories in configuration space. More precisely, we study the physics of the quantum switch (QS) interferometer within a Bohmian framework and show how the notion of causality is preserved in this approach. Furthermore, we investigate device-independent certification and causal inequalities applied to an entangled quantum system, and show that in this regime too, the notions of trajectories and of a strict causal order are perfectly preserved.
item.dc:creator: Aur\'elien Drezet

item.title: Experimenters' Free Will and Quantum Certainty
item.description: arXiv:1211.1917v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Physics has long lived with a split personality that desires determinism for measured systems while demanding that experimenters decide what to measure on a whim. Intriguingly, such a free will assumption for experimenters has thwarted many attempts to provide a satisfactory explanation of how quantum probabilities evolve to clear-cut measurements. An overview of this quantum measurement problem is presented without equations, and the lesson is drawn that denial of experimenters' free will may be the only workable solution. A holistic view is offered of a self-consistent superdetermined spacetime block universe of events. The goal of future research is to develop the underlying principle that generates this Escher-like global pattern.
item.dc:creator: Joseph J. Bisognano

item.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly -- Living with Priors in Bayesian confirmation
item.description: arXiv:2606.14281v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian confirmation faces a classic problem: where do initial priors come from? In cases with abundant data and repeated updating, different priors tend to converge to the same posterior. However, in frontier research this convergence often fails, and confirmation remains sensitive to priors. We examine how physics practice in the case of gravitational wave research deals with such cases and, normatively, when prior sensitivity should be regarded as epistemically problematic. We offer a practice-based account of the prior problem, drawn from a detailed case study in physics, of a kind so far absent from the philosophical literature on Bayesianism. One upshot is a clearer diagnosis of so-called `analogue confirmation'.
item.dc:creator: Niels Linnemann, Christian W\"uthrich
